paragraphs.text: Canon of John the Monk on Saint Basil, whose acrostic is: "With songs I sing Basil the Great." Ode 1. Tone 2. [Heirmos:] "By the wave of the sea." From heaven on high may you watch over us, divine, all-honoured and sacred head. May you guide our speech, and always steer our life toward what is more profitable. Like Paul, you had an unyielding desire to depart; but out of love for humankind you judged it more necessary to remain in the flesh for our sake, as the servant of the God who loves humankind. You were seen to be great in signs and wonders. By the fearful invocation of him who shattered the bronze gates of Hades you broke the iron bars, and you gave back to the faithful the church they had been deprived of. Your life, equal to the angels', ought to be honoured and crowned with the immaterial songs of the immaterial angels, as should the immaterial life in matter that you achieved on earth like an angel.

Theotokion. That crossing of ancient Israel through the sea painted your portrait beforehand. He walked across the watery deep without getting wet, just as you gave birth without seed, O all-blameless one. Ode 3. [Heirmos:] "You who [hung the earth] upon the waters." So that you might contain the whole radiance of the Holy Trinity, you separated your mind from every material impression, and you polished it with virtues like a translucent and most pure mirror. The company of monks had the good fortune to find in you a new Moses. They hold your words as divine laws, and your writings, which anoint them for ascetic struggle, as the tablets of Moses. You proclaimed the Father without beginning, the Son equally without beginning, and the Spirit; and you taught the one Godhead of the three hypostases, sharing one nature, for the Holy Trinity is one God. You strengthened the faith of the wise apostles for the orthodox, and when this preaching was besieged by preachings hostile to God, you fortified it, Basil. Theotokion. You, the cloud of light, O Maiden, made the Sun of glory rise from your womb with the rays of uncreated divinity. He appeared to all creation and abolished the deceit of godlessness. Ode 4. [Heirmos:] "The wicked one has heard." The most lawless king saw you standing upright before the sanctuary [?], wearing the diplois as the royal mantle of the divine priesthood, and he was shaken in his mind [?]. [?] the most dreadful [?] of the Holy Spirit [?], to call down a curse upon yourself if

you did not proclaim the Spirit itself as conjoined with the Father and the Son, as equal to them in honour by nature, and as consubstantial. You, Basil, had the mastery in wisdom and knowledge, far surpassing those who shared the same education. Next to your course and your way of life they seemed to run like men on foot beside a Lydian chariot, even when they thought they were keeping pace. You steered the Church like a merchant ship dreadfully tossed in the violent storm of heresies, and with the tiller of your words you rescued it from the surge of impiety and brought it to the calm harbour of orthodoxy. Theotokion. He who can blot out sins with a nod alone blotted out the great sin of the faithful woman, and through you he cast all her evils, from every side, into utter oblivion. Ode 5. [Heirmos:] "By the bond of love." All alike fell short of you in eloquence and virtue, blessed one, just as those who look up from every side simply fall short of heaven and the sun's ray. By the loftiness of your way of life you were seen to be a heaven. With heavenly, divine bread, your lofty word, Basil (for the Word is the bread of angels), you nourish souls that hunger for God and seek food that does not flow away, but rather remains forever. Turned inward and mostly lost in thought, thrice-blessed one, you always showed yourself plain and most frugal in dress and food: pale in appearance, grave in gait, silent, not quick to speak. Theotokion. Sanctified in soul and purified beforehand in body, O modest one, when the Holy Spirit came upon you, all-blameless one, you received the infinite power of the Most High overshadowing you. Ode 6. [Heirmos:] "He was held fast." You were seen to be an invincible champion of the orthodox, not of the heterodox. Pouring out your fiery tongue like a flaming sword, you hemmed in the enemies from the opposite side, and you wounded the bitter ruler of the power of the air, who is at work in it among the sons of disobedience. Faith is clearly the substance of things understood but not seen, and of things hoped for. Possessing it, you wisely disregarded the things that are seen, since they pass away, in your longing for the things that are not seen; for the things that are seen are temporary and fleeting, but the things that are not seen are eternal. You were seen to be high-minded, not low-minded, as you fought in defence of God, though for his sake you humbled yourself before all and fell at their feet. Though you were a creature of God, and yet commanded to become god, you refused to worship a creature as God, for God is the Creator of all.

You knew virtue in doing rather than in speaking, for, as he says, a silent deed is better than speech without action. You taught by doing more than by speaking; for whoever does and then teaches will be called great in heaven, the king[dom] of heaven [?]

Charioteer, travelling on high through the air, not mounted on fiery horses but riding the winged chariot of virtues, Basil, and driving toward the heavenly goal. Playing a pastoral tune on your shepherd's crook and on the rational pipe of your words, you gathered the sheep of the flock into one faith, into one place of green pasture, after they had escaped the thorny heresies. Let the new Paul, teacher of the Churches, who embraced all under heaven with his voice, the heavenly mind, the theological thunder and divine trumpet, Basil, be acclaimed. Anyone who carries your Hexaemeron on his tongue and fixes his mind on it is with the Creator. He comes to know the principles of creation and marvels at the Creator, using sight alone as his teacher. Theotokion. God, who formerly spoke to the fathers in many ways and in many portions, has in these latter times spoken to us in the Son. For his co-enthroned God the Word [?] came forth from you clothed in flesh, O Maiden. Ode 8. [Heirmos:] "Laws of the fathers." Rising like the sun, you scattered the deep and moonless night of dark heresies. You spread the golden rays of right faith over all and sowed the light of orthodoxy among those on earth, Basil; for darkness gives way to light, and falsehood yields to truth. You gathered varied flowers of divine knowledge from rational meadows, for you flew about the spiritual paradises of Scripture. Like a wise and industrious spiritual bee, you produced the mystical honey of theology. With it you blunted the bitterness of heresies and sweetened those who partake of it. Time and the grave, agents of forgetfulness, have given up their natural working, for they have no power over your sacred memory. Even though you have departed from here, blessed one, you live. For the righteous live in God, and after the end they live the life hidden in Christ; by your prayers make us partakers of it. Ephrem, the pillar of the desert, saw you as a pillar of fire reaching to heaven. Astonished at the vision, he came to the city of the Caesareans and found you addressing the people. There he beheld things more wondrous than the first: he saw in a mystery a white dove speaking at your ear. Theotokion. The bodiless one came forth from your womb bearing a body, O Lady: the Word of God the Father, who by his word established the bodiless nature and gave being to every begotten nature, rational and irrational. Therefore, Mother of Life, put to death the passions of my body, which deaden my mind. Ode 9. [Heirmos:] "Do not lament for me, Mother." Like a divine hierarch of God, holy Basil, you sacredly ministered the august and truly holy

Gospel of the kingdom, and you have received the reward of your sacred ministry, shown to be crowned even without a martyr's blood. He who set his tabernacle in the sun made his dwelling in you as in a vast heaven, as in a living sun, and as in the heavens [?]. For, he said of those like you, "I will dwell and walk among them" in a manner befitting God. You have run up from the things below to the fatherland above, and with the angels you stand before the dread throne of the super-essential Trinity, for whom you struggled on earth with all your strength. Remember us, holy one, and do not abandon those who remember you. You vigorously refuted the one who dared to bring down the form of the Godhead with himself, wickedly dragging the Master's [nature] into servitude, and, wretch that he was, setting down the timeless and uncreated nature as a creature with the

You have pierced the thick cloud of the flesh and paid back your loan to the earth, and now, with a soul set free and an immaterial mind, you have entered the formless darkness, there [?] to converse with God, to be with him and to rejoice with him. The Church of God is securely set on the unshakable foundation of your doctrines as on an unbreakable base and a firm rock. Unmoved by the hurricane blasts of contrary winds, it honours you with longing. Theotokion. You, all-holy Virgin, I faithfully put forward as an ambassador who will not be put to shame and a kindly mediator with the One born of you. I implore you: by your motherly intercessions utterly blot out the many multitudes of my many sins.

Canon of John the Monk on Chrysostom, whose acrostic is this: "Your namesake sings of you, O Golden Mouth. John, a wretched monk and suppliant." Tone 2. [Heirmos:] "By the wave of the sea, him who hid." With a mouth of clay and an earthy tongue I set out to hymn you, Chrysostom. Flash forth from heaven a gold-gleaming radiance of divine knowledge, and enlighten my mind and my heart. You passed by corruptible matter and fleeting glory, the whole world and the ruler of this world, and in place of them all you gained Christ, all-golden one. Wounded by love of him, you counted all things as rubbish. Obedient to the laws of Christ the Saviour, you took up your cross on your shoulders from your youth and followed him through the labours of ascesis, putting to death the mind of the flesh. You lived in trackless and waterless deserts, homeless, without possessions, without food, unknown, like the great Elijah and John the Forerunner. Emulating them, you emulated their boldness of speech [?]. Blessed one, you won a most splendid victory over the dragon and raised splendid trophies, like an Olympic victor. Then, borne by the divine Spirit, you hastened back to the city that had brought you up.

Ode 3. [Heirmos:] "You who [hung the earth] upon the waters." Enriched with the mind of Christ, you emulated his compassion as far as is possible for a human being, and you strove to save all through confession, abstinence from evil, and fervent repentance shown in deeds. God, your God, anointed you with the Holy Spirit, the oil of gladness and myrrh of divine anointing, above your fellows, and grace was poured out abundantly on your lips. You poured forth an ocean of the sweetest teachings, Chrysostom, drying up the filthy rain-torrents of heresies, muddy, undrinkable and briny, the hearts [?] ... [?] your mind has been shown purer than [?] every passionate and material thought, thrice-blessed Chrysostom; for in the crucible it has [?] purity. With the fiery rod of your all-golden teachings, through Christ, you made the surging sea of avarice passable by almsgiving, though it was impassable

He who before your birth knew the gold-gleaming brightness of your soul, and sanctified you before you were formed in the womb, holy all-golden one, clearly put you forward as another prophet Jeremiah, a sleepless shepherd and guardian of his flock. You were appointed by God, who entered into our poverty, as protector and champion of the poor and the common provider for the needy. Putting your all-golden tongue like a golden key into the storehouses and treasuries of the avaricious, you opened them to the poor. With intense speed and zeal, the fervent faith of pious emperors brought you from Antioch in Syria to the queen of cities and set you there, with very great glory, an escort and fitting honour, as one longed for, as an angel of God. The whole people of the city ran together as to a common feast and went out of the town as to a joyful festival. With applause they gladly

came to meet you, providing an escort to welcome you on your arrival. Theotokion. You alone in all generations are, beyond nature, called both Virgin and Mother, O Lady. You bore a pre-eternal and timeless infant, born of the Father without a mother before all things, and from you, a mother, after all things, without a father, conceived [?] as he knows.

Ode 6. ... Like a gold-shining, gold-gleaming sun, you rose as a bridegroom from his chamber on the height of the Church. With the golden rays of your teaching you gilded all creation, and with a mystical spring you scattered the heavy winter of heresies. The emperor, the people and the choir of priests were astonished as they clearly saw the testimony to your bright and pure life brought from above. For the faithful witness in heaven, who knows all things, bore witness to the beauty of your ways. Your lips became a mystical lyre of the Holy Spirit and a melodious harp. They sang an all-harmonious song, a musical ode, a clear-sounding echo, charming and delighting souls with the rhythmic sweetness of the composition and the grace of the interwoven sounds. By your oratory you persuaded countless people to become friends of God and workers of virtue. Blessed one, you are a mountain dripping sweetness, a divine dew falling from heaven and enriching the fields of souls. Therefore your words seemed to the peoples sweeter than honey, Chrysostom. Theotokion. Fertile mountain, all-golden lampstand, jar of the manna of [?], gilded gate, unburnt fire-bearing bush, living throne, heaven full of light, renowned seat of Christ, gold-woven bridal chamber, spring of fragrance, tabernacle of God, O Lady,

Ode 7. [Heirmos:] "Ineffable wonder." Watered by the frequent showers and rains of your words like rich and fertile land, the Church has been shown to be abundantly fruitful, bearing the fruit of various virtues

Out of a clear sky bright with day, a night of despondency and a darkness of dejection suddenly covered the bride of Christ when she lost you, her great luminary, through the malice of the ruler of [?] ... Ravening wolves condemned you, the good shepherd. They wore the faces of shepherds and sheep's skin outwardly, but hid the fox within and covered the beast with the fleece. Like a grief-stricken and tearful widow, the Church groaned bitterly, Chrysostom, seeking you, her bridegroom. Because of the widow, she suffered this untimely widowhood. Theotokion. He who alone judges righteousness has sat upon a throne, O Lady. Taking flesh from you, he showed you to be a fiery throne, and so he sits in your bosom as on a holy throne, as befits an infant.

[?] the imitator of the Lamb, like a lamb and a notable ram, and like a rational lamb that does not cry out at all, the shepherds and wolves seized you with murderous hands and exiled you far from your flock [?]

Mountains and glens, hills, valleys, ravines, seas and rivers, stars, moon and sun, heaven and earth, and all creation grew gloomy, rebuking the lawlessness then committed by unjust elders. Another paralytic found in you, the disciple of Christ, another Christ, and he at once found healing as well. For as soon as you spoke [?], he immediately rose, took up his [?], and walked away rejoicing and magnifying Christ. So that those who live in the night of ignorance might behold the light of knowledge, and those who worship the visible sun might learn that the sun is [a creature?] of the one God, you were sent like Paul to the distant nations, scattering the mist of unbelief like a sun. Theotokion. From you, O Mother of God, came forth clothed in flesh, as from a living bridal chamber, the Wisdom of God, the truly unvarying image of the Father, the living and unmoved seal, the exact imprint, the Only-begotten, and in his love for humankind he lived among human beings. Ode 9 is missing.

John the Monk, on Saint Nicholas of Myra. Ode 3. [Heirmos:] "You who [hung the earth] upon the waters." [Cod. f. 107.] Myra of Lycia brought you forth like precious myrrh, sacred minister Nicholas, perfuming the senses of souls with the flowers of graces and the spices of virtues. The whole world has you, Nicholas, as swift help in afflictions, comfort in sorrows, consolation in calamities, a champion in temptations, and a medicine that soothes pain in sickness. You were nourished on the words of the faith and from infancy you drank the rational and pure milk of piety. So you truly attained, blessed one, to the perfect man and to the measure of the stature of Christ. Following in the footsteps of the Saviour, you were not a hireling but rather a good shepherd. You laid down your life for your sheep and fulfilled the Gospel of Christ in deeds. Theotokion. The bush wrapped in fire foreshowed you, all-praised one. The jar that held the manna prefigured you, the God-receiving table, O most pure one; for you have poured forth undefiled sweetness for us. Ode 4. [Heirmos:] "Your [...] on the cross." Your soul was full of mercy and kindness. You cheerfully shared your wealth with those in need, putting on a heart of compassion like the great

Looking to the star that never sets, you steered the ship of your mind by its movements and brought it to a calm harbour, like the best helmsman of the sea[?]. With the great courage of divine strength, calling on Christ, you set free those who were bound in prison, blessed one, and led them out. Your heart was full of the Holy Spirit, and it breathed forth a sweet fragrance, an aromatic scent, mingled with radiance and blended with light. Theotokion. The poverty of mortal minds cannot explain your birth, which surpasses thought. Its account is entirely ineffable, and its manner, O Virgin, beyond understanding. Ode 5. [Heirmos:] "To you I rise early." With your sweet words you persuaded many who hated the turmoil of the world to break away from the world and cling to the Master who calls them to divine delights above the world. Girded with divine strength and might and fenced about with [?] full armour, you were not wounded by the darts of Belial; rather, you wounded his utterly profane heart. You built the four virtues into a four-horse chariot, a fire-bearing vehicle, and ascended to heaven, where Christ ascended before as forerunner, to be seen before his face. Like divine salt, blessed one, you were cast into the whole world, stopping the rot of despondency, drying up the flow of afflictions, and gathering and binding together slackened souls. Theotokion. Without leaving his Father's bosom, Christ God sits in your motherly bosom, O Virgin. He who is without a mother came forth from you without a father. And Abraham's bosom again

Ode 6. [Heirmos:] "He was held fast but not held down." You obeyed, and did not disobey, blessed one, the divine command that says, "Do not let your left hand know what your right hand is doing." Indeed, you went far beyond it: you did not even admit the very man you were helping as a partner in your plan or a sharer in your purpose. You proved to be one who uproots every evil, not one who cultivates it. Plant in me, Father, flourishing and thick-leaved stems, shady and abundant shoots of virtues and sacred graces. Uproot my thorny growth and the passionate side-shoots

Longing to attain heavenly and not earthly glory, you disregarded the glory that drags downward, since it passes away and dissolves. It is like a shadow and resembles a dream; it has no substance and is plainly like smoke scattering into the air. I have defiled my flesh, O Christ, and not nailed it down with fear of you. Like the profane fornicator Esau, I have dissolved purity in lust, and I have made my sanctified members the profane members of a harlot. Therefore, by the prayers of your Nicholas, again

Theotokion. You were shown to be higher and loftier than visible and spiritual creation, O Maiden, for you hold in your hands the One who holds creation together, like a fiery throne. Implore him to redeem me from the confinement [?] of Hades and from bitter distress, and from the hardness of heart that now holds me fast. Ode 7. [Heirmos:] "Ineffable." Three daughters with their father were in danger of falling into the utmost Charybdis of evils and dying an eternal death, but you brought them to anchor in the harbour of immortal life and of the kingdom. Your pure heart had the Sun of glory dwelling in it, wise one, and it shone wholly with immaterial light, clearly sharing its own radiance with those who saw it. With the sling of God-woven doctrines you drove the pestilent and savage wolves far from your flock, holy one, and kept your people unharmed by the frenzied babbling of Arius. As Paul says, the whole world has been crucified to you, as you were crucified with Christ, who was crucified and by his cross undid the ancient cur[se]

Theotokion. Virgin Mother, nursing an infant conceived without seed, you alone on earth were shown to be Lady. Through him Israel drank a new drink from the sheer, hard and waterless rock, and sucked oil and

Ode 8. [Heirmos:] "Laws of the first [fathers]." You appeared, blessed one, as a pillar of fire reaching to heaven, going before the nation that bears the name of Christ and leading the new Israel. You enlightened the tribes that followed you and shaded them with the dew-bearing cloud of grace, but you filled the ranks of the heterodox with fog and mist, smoke and gloom. Walking by the laws of the Chief Shepherd, you were not a hireling, Father, but a good shepherd. You laid down your life for your sheep, and in laying down your own life for us you imitated God the Word, who in his love for humankind poured out his precious blood for the ungrateful. Relief of the despondent, swift help of mourners, ready protector of the world and prompt aid, you were seen as a gold-gleaming sun, riding the four-horse chariot of the virtues, wise one, and borne on the gold-rimmed chariot of graces. With the radiance of wonders and the flash of good deeds you kindle and light up [?] every soul, thrice-blessed one, dispelling the gloom of despondency with the light of good cheer, joy and gladness. Your struggles and toils, the vapours of your labours and your sweat, like compounded incense

…and, offered to Christ as precious myrrh for a fragrant odour, they have set you in the world as a river of sanctification, a spring of divine myrrh and a sea of wonders, Nicholas, sacred initiate. Theotokion. — Beyond cause and beyond thought, O Maiden, you gave a body to the Word who came forth from the uncaused Father and is the cause of all that exists. He had you as the cause when he took flesh from you, so that he might save mankind, since he loves mankind by nature. For mankind's sake he willingly became man and, in his love for mankind, lived among men. Ode 9. "Do not lament for me." Be merciful to me, O Saviour, on the day of judgement, when I stand naked before your judgement seat. Then look on me with a merciful eye at the intercessions of the divine Nicholas, for you alone are truly good and

Because you loved the meekness of Moses, who saw God, you also inherited the glory of his countenance. For even after death your face [shone?] with radiant beams of immaterial light and with the sweetest brightness [?]…

With the lever of your prayers, and with the cross as a mighty weapon that shakes down walls, you prised the polluted shrines of the most abominable gods up from their foundations. In their place, blessed one, you raised holy houses to Christ, who alone is properly and by nature God. Your mind was a sleepless, godly-minded eye and a spiritual lamp, burning with virtues and always richly supplied with the abundant oil of almsgiving. So you have entered into the joy of the Lord.

Your mind was master of your appetites, Father, and so you mightily withstood the enemy who rules this world, for the Almighty was your helper. Having reigned over the passions, you stood by night before the emperor Constantine, the sovereign. Neither the sand of the seashore nor the multitude of the waves, neither the drops of dew and the fine flakes of snow, nor the choir of the stars, nor the drops of rain, nor flowing rivers, nor the streams of springs will ever equal your wonders, Father. Theotokion. — The Son and Word of God, coeternal with the Father, was born of you as Son of Man and made the sons of men sons of God by grace, O Maiden. Ask him to make me too, a son of Gehenna, a son of God.

Ode 1 [?]. Grave tone. "At your nod toward the earthly…" [Cod. f. 10[?].] Longing only for the enjoyment of the good things to come, wise one, you ran past the things that flow away. So you were joined to Christ and blended with him in a fiery love, made wholly glowing by immaterial and divine fire.

Theotokion. — By your all-immaculate childbearing, Mother of God, paradise has been opened, which our first mother closed long ago, and the ancient homeland has been given back to the human race. Ode 3. "He who in the beginning…" Though you travelled on foot [?], you were shown to be an eagle coursing on the clouds. In the twinkling of an eye, by the all-working and divine Spirit, you came on a cloud from Rome to Zion to bury the living cloud.

"What God has cleansed," he who alone is pure by nature, "let no man call common," he says. For to the pure all the works of God are pure. Therefore, Peter, cleanse me of impure passions by your intercessions

Theotokion. — You are my mighty refuge and my protection, ready to save, Lady. I fervently implore and beseech you: [deliver?] my soul when it is separated from its tent and departs from the earth to another world. Ode 4. "The paternal…" You ran ahead of all the disciples to the tomb of the Life who is a person. I sleep in the tomb of stony hardness of heart: raise me up through repentance. The mind grows dizzy when it considers your journeys over sea and land, the sweat and the toils that you gladly endured for the gospel of grace. I have grown wholly old in evils and gone lame in both legs, straying from the paths of God. Holy one, make me sound, for I limp on the way to virtue. You received from Christ the Church, which the Lord himself set up, and not men, and you steered it well like a merchant ship, from [?]…

…pure, chosen and blameless, whom Christ God, incomparable in beauty, loved: I implore you, Lady, save me. Ode 5. "O Lord my God." Let the guardian of Rome, the keeper of the kingdom's treasury, the rock of the faith, the firm foundation of the catholic Church, be praised in sacred songs. Long ago, Peter, you asked Christ whether you should forgive those who sin against you as many as seven times, and you heard: "I do not say to you seven times, but rather seventy times seven." "Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints," as it is written. But your death, all-praised one, is truly far more precious, since it bore the seal [?] of the divine passion

Every infirmity and every disease was driven from the believers by your healing hands [?]. You laid them on the sick and made them well, apostle. Theotokion. — Theotokos, you exalted the humbled nature of mankind and raised it from the ancient fall, for you gave birth to Christ, who sets upright those who have been dashed to the ground. Ode 6. "Seasick…" Peter, you dissolved into nothing and destroyed the false signs and phantom powers of Simon the accursed, as the sun dissolves darkness and mist, and you worked many mighty deeds in God. The Wisdom of God, which has authority over all things, gave you too, Peter, authority to tread on scorpions and serpents, both visible and invisible. [Deliver?] me from their venomous wickedness. And rather, Peter, your most beautiful fe[et]…

OF JOHN THE MONK, whose acrostic is: "I hymn the contests of George the martyr." Praise of John. Ode 1. Plagal fourth tone. "The charioteer…" [Cod. f. 155.] You tilled the ploughland of your mind with the cross and sowed virtues in it with tears, and now you reap rejoicing. For through martyrdom, George, you have grown an ever-living ear of grain that nourishes souls. In the violent surge of impiety you stood, renowned one, like an unbroken rock and an unshaken tower. With the noble stature of your steadfast heart you broke the waves of torments into foaming bubbles. The righteous man is as confident as a lion, and so you appeared. Having ruled royally over ignoble passions, you rushed fearlessly into the arena like a lion and terrified your enemies with your royal roar, as though they were worthless foxes. Martyr, you checked the stream of deceit as it was carried along unrestrained. Its seething and most violent force dashed furiously on you and broke vehemently against you, but you were like an indestructible barrier and forced it to retreat.

Theotokion. — A slow tongue, a plainly feeble voice and a harsh-sounding mouth are afraid to address hymns to you, Lady. For you are hymned by all the fiery and flame-formed tongues of the angels and by the mouths of the bodiless ones. Ode 3. "He who established…" To attain the glory and the life hidden in Christ, you despised the glory that passes away and rightly disregarded corruptible life. So through death you found eternal life. You did not grow numb with toil, nor did you weary at all as you fought against fire and iron. You were firmer than iron and every adamant, and you endured as though you were watching someone else suffer. For Christ's sake you grappled [?] with instruments of torture which [cut?] you into parts and divided your body limb by limb into small pieces, much-contending one. Yet you kept your mind uncut from the love of Christ. You were scourged for Christ, who was scourged for you, and you glorified him in your limbs. Since you bore his marks in your own flesh, you were glorified in return all the more, glorified George. Theotokion. — A storm of sins, a towering wave of transgressions and reefs of wickedness, one after another, drive me into the deep abyss of despair. Give me your hand, Virgin, so that the wave does not cover me alive. Ode 4. "You are my Lord, O Christ." You spat on rhetorical quibbling and on the drivel of the unwise, who battle against the truth and against one another with contentious antitheses. Wise and shrewd as you were, George, you loved the wisdom of Christ God with your whole soul. Typhoon-like blasts of violent tortures, most bitter rivers of scourges and a turbid, fiery rain assailed you together and burst suddenly on you, but they did not topple the tower of your confession, for it had been founded on the rock. When they kindled a furnace for you with much fuel, you ran into it as into a dewy bridal chamber. For a divine angel came down and, whistling through it like a breath of dew, made the fury of the furnace [?]. He shook out the flame and showed you to be stronger than fire. All-renowned one, you carried on your tongue the word of God, which is living and gives life, and by prayer you brought back to life a dead pagan who had died before Christ came down. You baptized him with divine baptism and set him free from the Gehenna of fire.

…lamented bitterly. And [?] God, the herald of God, with a human voice [?] was ground to dust [?]. You could not bear to see God insulted by lawless rulers. Your heart was kindled with divine zeal, and you came forward and refuted the great deceit of those who had gone astray, and confessed Christ as God. Of your martyrdom, O Saviour, you sang [?], having run [?] the way, and I shall be delighted, in being nailed [?] the

[?] a statue and an image of God, surpassingly lovely in its beauty [?]. The hands that fashioned man with great wisdom and skill carved you and shaped you harmoniously into unspeakable beauty. Theotokion. — A roaring lion prowls around, seeking to swallow me with his teeth. All-blameless one, do not give me to him as prey, you who bore God, who crushed the lions' teeth with his mighty divine hand. Ode 6. "I will pour out my prayer." You proclaimed as Word of God and God the one who stretched out his hands on the wood and had his side dug by the lance. And you, George, were hung on the wood and had your sides pierced with pikes, but by prayer [you blunted?] their points…

He was more senseless than stones, so senseless that he worshipped senseless stones. He stretched you out on your back on the ground, struck you with a stone and crushed your entrails. But you longed for the Rock of life, the precious stone, Christ. The son of Gehenna, himself tinder for the unquenchable fire, buries you, martyr, in freshly burned, seething quicklime. But as usual you found an angel guarding you, the one who has delivered you from your youth. You proved stronger than iron, stone, bronze and adamant, George. Each of these things gives way to fire and is consumed, but you, by great grace, prevailed even over all-devouring fire. Theotokion. — Beyond thought, nature and reason you bear without a father the one who is without a mother, so that he might make man god by adoption. I fell through hoping for godhead: Lady, make me too worthy of his sweet beauty. Ode 7. "The youths from Judea…" Nothing could harm or injure you, the soldier of God: not boiling cauldrons, not the gaping jaws of lions. For God will not hand over to beasts a soul that confesses him. Martyr George, you used reason to arbitrate between your soul and your flesh, and you wisely subjected the body to the spirit, the worse to the better, proving an exact judge of what each deserved. Famous prize-winner, rich in great boldness before the Saviour, scatter the wealth of my passions and the load of my evils, I pray, and grant me respite and relief from the burden. Let the martyr be praised in hymns, great in understanding and abundant in wisdom. In words he exposed the idle deceit, in deeds he triumphed over it, and he proclaimed Christ the Son and Word of God. Theotokion. — Be my protectress, be my bright helper, Mother of God, when the last and great crisis overtakes my soul, and deliver me from the hand of the robbers who travel through the air. Ode 8. "Sevenfold the furnace…" Athanasius, the bright namesake of immortality, found immortality through you. At the tyrant's command he had mixed a death-bringing drug for you, but seeing that you had drunk it unharmed,

he was amazed and recognized the power of Christ, who destroyed death by death. Girded from heaven with invincible strength and might, you endured being whirled around on the wheel. You were cut by swords, your fibres and sinews were torn out, the joints of your bones were broken all around, and all your holy fingers were reaped like ears of grain. Your hands and feet were lacerated with rawhide thongs, but you hamstrung the enemy, whose neck is plainly a sinew of iron. For Christ gave you sinew as you fought for him, putting sinews of bronze about you, as Scripture says, and breathing into you the power to do mighty deeds in God and to undo the power of darkness. You persuaded even the demons, against their will, to confess that Christ is God and Lord of all creation and Creator of human nature, though by nature they plainly love lies. For they feared your authority over them, and like slaves who deserve the whip they carried out your commands. Theotokion. — The fleshless one took flesh from your all-pure blood, O Virgin. Man had been subjected to fleshly desires and had come to have no share in the Spirit, but he strengthened him by the gift of the Holy Spirit [?] to keep the unruly body under and to bring it into subjection. Ode 9. "Every ear was astonished." You set your spiritual [thoughts?] firmly on the rock of faith and ground the idols of deceit to dust. Bowing your neck to God and to the sword, you had your head cut off, contestant, [and went?] to the Head of all

Like a snow-bright lily you blossomed in the valleys of the martyrs. Reddened with the divine gore of your contest, you became a red rose, fragrant and breathing myrrh, and on all you breathed the heavenly scent of Christ's sufferings. Your much-contending body alone proved firmer than any iron, George, for the hammers of torture left no mark on it. It had first been forged in the fire of the love of Christ, and then it was tempered in your hot blood as though dipped in cold water. By the grace of Christ, who conquered the world, as he said, you conquered the powers and man-hating principalities of the ruler of this world. Then, a trophy-bearing athlete, you went up from earth to heaven to be crowned by the right hand that gives victory. The wonders [?] that you worked while you lived, and still work after your end, equal the streams of rivers. For the righteous truly live in God even after death, since their souls are in the hand of God. I have no fluency of speech, nor a hymn-writing tongue able to honour all your countless [deeds] fittingly. So accept these words, beauty of the martyrs: I turn and implore Christ my Saviour to be merciful to me. The Theotokion is missing.

CANON TO SAINT BLAISE, whose acrostic is: "I, John, hymning the shoots of the labours of Blaise." Ode 1. Plagal fourth tone. "The charioteer…" [Cod. f. 172b.] Truly, Blaise, you subjected the irrational passions to reason, their ruler. You scorned the king's command and word and proclaimed the King whose rule passes to no successor and whose kingdom is eternal. Word of God, give me wisdom as I open my mouth to hymn Blaise, who is truly holy. For you gave him wisdom, and his opponents could not withstand it. Father, you became a fruitful branch of the life-giving Vine, bearing virtues like ripe clusters. You were cut [?] with the sword and trodden by feet that were not beautiful, and so, Blaise, you poured out wines of compunction for all. Your deeds clearly showed you to be like the great Job: true, meek, compassionate and just, pious and blameless, truly keeping away from every evil deed, glory of the priest-martyrs. Theotokion. — Let us call blessed, in a manner fitting holy things, the most honoured rod that sprang from the root of Jesse and blossomed [?] Christ, the truly unfading flower: the holy Virgin, the living city of God. Ode 3. "Of the heavenly…" Those who wished to take you captive for an unjust slaughter were themselves taken captive by you for eternal life. They were brought to God the Almighty as a catch far more precious than irrational animals. Your wonders outnumber the sand of the sea, wise one. For you end incurable afflictions of souls and bodies: you dispel diseases and inflammations of the throat, and you dry up discharges of the pharynx. The great [?] of Sebaste… as… [?] Through intense vigil and prayer you became a place [?], a mountain for the Lord and God of Jacob. For the Trinity dwelt in your heart as in a holy tabernacle [?]

Theotokion. — Lady, we know you as the spiritual tongs that hold Christ, the true coal, in your arms. With him burn up my passions, which are like brushwood, and cleanse my mind, which has grown wild like a thicket. Ode 4. "I have heard, O Lord." You rose above the senses and turned away from the utterly shameful [?], flying on the golden wings of priesthood and of contest. You became a vessel of the myrrh of the Holy Spirit and the fragrance of Christ, and you breathed out [?] the scent of his knowledge and of his sufferings. [?] a means of deliverance, a thing that puts evil spirits to flight, an unbearable terror to demons and a heavy scourge: such is your name. As a shepherd you shepherded the flock, while you yourself were shepherded from above like a sheep. And to him who lays down [his life] like a sheep you were offered as a ram, most sacred one. Theotokion. — Him who cannot be contained by all things, without constriction

you contained, O Maiden, and so became more spacious than the heavens, beyond understanding. And like a good trainer of children, [?] children and infants free from care… Why [?]… you brought [?] pure and spotless lambs, offered as whole burnt offerings through fire [?]. You lightened every toil and healed every infirmity and disease, curing by prayer and touch those who ran to you. For you had received freely, and you gave freely to all, as a most genuine disciple of Christ. Blaise, the fruit of your labours sprouted an ear of martyrdom. It was reaped by the sickle of tortures, gathered into the storehouses of heaven and became the purest bread for the Master. Theotokion. — Now, all-pure one, all generations call you blessed, for you are blessed. For the blessed [?] Master, rescuing me from the tyranny of demons, appeared through you as the lover of mankind.
As once [you drew out] the fishbone that had stuck fast in the child's throat, so now [draw out] by your touch the thorn of pleasures, which stands like a sharp dart in the throat of my soul [?]…

You stripped off the garments of skin, which belong to mortality, and the passion of corruption. Laying aside your robe, you were clothed with glory by being stripped. For you were bound naked, on your back [?], and your sides were furrowed with claws. The softness and weakness of womankind were strengthened by the firmness of your contests and grappled manfully with the enemy. For they stood firm even to the point of blood against wicked sin, contending beyond the power of nature. You begot those women in bonds, as Paul did, and through your prayers he who wills all men to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth steeled them and strengthened them to stand against sword and scourges and fire. Theotokion. — The Builder of heaven found you on earth, Mother of God, as a dwelling higher than the height of heaven. He came forth like a bridegroom from the light-bearing chamber of your womb, the God of the heavens and of all flesh, having wedded flesh to himself. Ode 7. "The youths from Judea…" You carried the divine cross as a strong staff for your old age. When you were beaten with rods, the rod of piety now and your staff [?]… and comforted me. The all-devouring mouth of the wolf, with a bridle [?]… supplies by divine grace, and the mist of diseases by the radiance of wonders

[?] they lost, they sank into the deep, and they suffered that which they had done [?], having cast many [?] under [?] Christ as shepherd [?], as now the soldiers who [?] trusted in them, the truly deranged, the truly [?]

[?] a divine angel flew down [?] … "Rejoice" [?] … kissing [?] you graciously and [?] "Arise, and receive with joy as a gift the crown of glory prepared for you." Being earth, clay and mire, the tyrant thinks earthly thoughts and reasons in worldly terms [?] the great marvel of Christ's power… dedicating [?] to rotten demons incurably… for to name as saviour [?] those who had perished earlier through weak parents [?]. Theotokion. — The Creator of human nature dwelt in your womb, Lady, because it was pure, and he drove out the ancestral [transgression?] that had dwelt in us. Those who had long ago been bitterly exiled from the delightful paradise he settled there again, glorifying him. Ode 9. "He was amazed…" I am always wallowing like a pig in the slime and mire of sins and chasing a dissolute life and pleasure that flows away, and so I lie as prey for the spiritual wolf. Through God's servant may I be rescued from his hunting, so that I do not become his food. Beautiful are your feet, sacred celebrant, for you proclaimed the peace that surpasses all understanding and things beyond thought, Blaise, before the tyrant's tribunal [?]… Standing in many waters, you made your paths, and your footprints were not known. With the noose of fasting you also strangled gluttony [?], an insatiable beast, a bitter Scylla, the many-headed Hydra of myth. From this you received the grace to draw out painlessly, by the divine touch of your relics, bones stuck in the chest and throat. … [?] who for a long time suffered one disease after another, dragging out a wretched life full of suffering; for [?] of matter [?] always carried along,

…faultily of the mind, it besieges me, it wears me down violently, [?] with many pains… Since you have a fountain of healings, being rich in the working of miracles before God as the prize of your venerable contests, you painlessly soothe the ailments of wounds and the inflammations in the throat, and you quietly scatter them by your visitations… [?] The prayer that you prayed to the Master, Father, at the time of your death, pray now as well, that we who call upon you may have you as our helper, deliverer and aid in griefs, in hardships, in sicknesses, in dangers, troubles and trials. Theotokion. — The Savior and Master and Redeemer beyond word and mind and understanding, … [?] O Lady, who gave birth to him in the body, from my passions … [?]

"At that time Jesus went through the grainfields on the Sabbath, and his disciples were hungry and began to pluck heads of grain and…"

"And your servant," it says, "and your beast of burden shall rest on the Sabbath": that is, in this life of seven days. The body, as the beast of burden, shall cease from the slavery of sin and [?] shall serve the divine commandments; and anger and desire, as the servant, shall cease from sin and be allowed to devote themselves to God: desire stretching wholly toward God, and anger arming itself against the enemies of God.

"And he was transfigured before them, and his face shone like the sun, and his garments became white as the light."

The Lord is transfigured, not by taking on what he was not, but by revealing to the disciples what he was. And his face shines like the sun (for it is identified with another light by hypostasis [?]), while his garments become white as snow, according to Mark. For the clothing is glorified by relation, not by hypostatic union. Just as the sun is one but has two substances, the light, which came into being first, and the body set high above creation, and the light is indivisibly united throughout the whole body, and while the body remains where it is, the light spreads over all the earth…

…to intelligible beings, God (…), and the garments become white as light, made splendid by sharing in the divine light. That it did not shine merely like the sun, but that the light was even greater than the comparison, the disciples showed by falling down. For if the light had not been unmixed, but only matching the sun, they would not have fallen.

"This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; listen to him."

Note that earlier, at the Jordan, the Trinity was attested when the Son was baptized, the Father bearing witness from above and the Spirit descending like a dove. Now on Tabor the same Trinity is attested again: in the one who proclaims, in the one who is proclaimed, and in the Spirit in the cloud. This is what David foretold: "Tabor and Hermon shall rejoice in your name." For Hermon rejoiced when Christ was baptized, and Tabor when he was transfigured, since on both occasions a voice came, saying, "This is my Son."

"And he took the cup, and when he had given thanks he gave it to them, saying, Drink from it, all of you."

The bread and wine are not a figure of the body and blood of Christ (God forbid!), but the very body itself and the very blood itself. They pass into the strengthening of our soul and body, not consumed, not corrupted, not passing into the drain, but into our substance and preservation. And if some have called the bread and wine antitypes of the Lord's body and blood, they did not say so after the consecration, but before it, calling the offering by that name. They are called antitypes of things to come, not because they are not truly the body and blood of Christ, but because now we share through them in the divinity of Christ, whereas then we will share in it spiritually, through sight alone. It is called partaking because through it we partake of the divinity of Jesus; and communion because through it we have communion with Christ and share in both his flesh and his divinity. Through it we also have communion and are united with one another. For since we all partake of one bread, we become one body of Christ and one blood, and members of one another, being called of one body with Christ.

"And throwing down the pieces of silver in the temple, he departed, and went and hanged himself."

Of the kinds of abandonment, one is for the sake of a hidden virtue, so that it may be revealed, as with Job; another is to ward off pride, as with Paul; another is for the correction of someone else, as with Lazarus and the rich man, for when we see others suffering we are naturally humbled. Another is for the glory of someone else, as with the man blind from birth, for the glory of Christ. Another is to rouse others to zeal, as in martyrdom. And in short, there are two kinds of abandonment: there is providential and educative abandonment, and there is complete abandonment, beyond hope. Providential and educative abandonment is that which happens for the correction, salvation and glory of the one who suffers, or for the zeal and imitation of others, or for the glory of God. Complete abandonment is when God has done everything for a man's salvation, and the man remains incurable by his own choice. Then he is handed over to destruction, like Judas.

"And over his head they put the charge against him, written: This is Jesus, the King of the Jews."

The writing on the whitened board that Pilate fixed above the Lord's head fulfilled the Lord's word, when he said, "When I am lifted up, I will draw all people to myself." So the reading posted there showed that the saving Passion took place not for Judea alone, but for the whole Greek and barbarian world as well.

"Now from the sixth hour there was darkness over all the land until the ninth hour."

The sun is eclipsed when the body of the moon comes in between like a dividing wall and casts a shadow, not allowing the light to reach us. As much of the sun as the moon is found to hide, so great is the eclipse. The eclipse of the moon is caused by the shadow of the earth, when the moon is fifteen days old and is found directly opposite at the extreme point, the sun beneath the earth and the moon above it. For the earth casts a shadow, and the sun's light cannot reach the moon to illuminate it, and so the moon is eclipsed.

"And behold, I am with you always, to the end of the age. Amen."

He said he would be not only with them, but also with all who would believe after them. For the apostles were certainly not going to remain until the end of the age; but he speaks to the faithful as to a single body. "Do not tell me," he says, "how difficult the task is. For I am with you, making everything easy." He said this constantly to the prophets too in the Old Testament: to Jeremiah when he pleaded his youth, and to Moses, and to Ezekiel when they shrank back: "I am with you." So too here, to these men. But notice here the difference between them. The prophets, sent to a single nation, often

begged to be excused; these men said nothing of the kind, though they were being sent to the whole world. In many places in Scripture the word "until" indicates the limit of a fixed time, but does not deny what comes after. It is said, for example, of the ever-virgin Mother of God that Joseph did not know her until she had given birth to her firstborn son; and one must certainly not suppose that afterward she accepted union with a man. So here too the Lord promised to be with us until the end, not as though he would be separated from us after the end of the age. Indeed, the divine Apostle says that after the general resurrection "we shall be caught up in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air, and so we shall always be with the Lord." He also reminds them of the end in order to draw them on all the more, so that they might look not only at the unpleasantness of the present, but also at the endless good things to come. "For the sorrows," he says, "that you will endure in the present life will be dissolved along with it, since this age itself will come to its end; but the good things you will enjoy remain immortal." Having thus anointed and roused their minds, he also sent them out with the remembrance of that day. For that day is longed for by those who live in good deeds, just as it is fearful to those who live in sins, as it is to the condemned. But let us not merely fear and tremble; let us also change while there is time, undergoing the good transformation, so that we may enjoy eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom be glory and power, together with the Father who has no beginning and the life-giving Spirit, now and always and to the ages of ages. Amen.

TO CONSTANTINE, THE MOST HOLY POPE OF ROME. A defense concerning the things set in motion against the holy and ecumenical sixth council in the time of the tyranny of Vardan [read: Bardanes].

To the most holy in all things and blessed brother and fellow minister, the lord Constantine, John, bishop: greetings in the Lord.

God, who wrought the great works in the visible world as a token of his own divinity and power, displayed the marks of his own glory and wisdom above all in the most honored part of sensible creation, I mean in our own fashioning; which is why the Prophet cried out that the knowledge of God has been made wonderful from himself. He, the Creator of our nature, skillfully set the head at the front of the whole body and placed in it the most vital of the senses, and he caused all the movement and soundness of the other members to come about and be preserved from there. And if any of these…

…should happen to stumble or be harmed in some other way, the head does not treat their care as no concern of its own. Rather, showing its natural sympathy even toward the furthest members, it heals what is suffering through the service of the hands under the guidance of the eye, not despising them and dismissing their cooperation as useless. To these things, most holy ones, we may compare the matters of your apostolic primacy. And since we reckon you, in accordance with the canons, as the head of the priesthood of Christ, we fittingly seek through you to receive consolation for the despondency that has befallen our ecclesiastical body from a pestilent, soul-sickening tyrannical power. For surely you too, by the very nature of the head, will not overlook us who have fallen sick against our will, nor will you cast us out of our natural union with you. Rather, grieving over our wounds (for when one member suffers, it is natural that all the members suffer with it, as the Apostle says), you will now most rightly rejoice with us at our return to health and our restoration to soundness; especially since the illness did not originate from any cause within the body, but was the result of a violent and unexpected calamity from outside. Concerning this, God-honored brothers, we have of necessity sent you the present letter of information, laying bare, as it were, and showing you through it how grievous the wound was. That is why until now we were prevented from coming to your holiness with the customary synodical address, held as we were under tyranny; for there was no other way for us to write to you while setting out the doctrines of true religion purely and without contamination. For the man who, like a bandit and as if from an ambush, inflicted this wound upon us, having seized this God-guarded city with outside force (I would not truly call it imperial rule), for reasons known to the Providence that governs all things (for indeed

it is not for us to search out the depths of the divine judgments), and putting forward violence and lawlessness as the foundation and base of his power, tore down, even before he entered, the image of the holy sixth council that had been set up in the forecourts of the palace. He wanted to install on the throne of the high priesthood a man who did not belong to our ecclesiastical body but shared his own perverse opinion; but he was forced by the vehemence and resistance of our pious clergy, and so promoted us to the dignity and summit of the high priesthood, though we did not expect it, did not want it, and did not endure it without suffering, distress and every kind of lament. For who, being wholly inexperienced in sailing the sea, would board a ship and agree to cross a strait (to say nothing of setting out on a voyage across the open ocean), when he alone was to be entrusted with the vessel's tiller and was taking on the steering of himself and of all who sailed with him? Anyone who sees this in our case (for we were never among those practiced in what is most fitting and proper for hierarchs, nor did we hold any distinction in the ranks of the Church, but devoted ourselves unceasingly to the service of the mysteries alone) will not find it hard to believe that our mind was unwilling in this matter, since we put forward, as proof of the truth of what we say, the very testimony of our conscience, which the divine Apostle declared to be his boast. This man, then, making the disorder of the Church his own ornament, was in labor and eager to give birth to the basilisk of impiety, the offspring of the serpent who is the author of evil: so that publicly in the churches and in the professions of faith of the bishops the aforementioned holy sixth council should be subjected to anathema, together with the forefathers of your apostolic and venerable see, all who championed the pious doctrine of truth; and so that all should jointly confess in incongruous terms that had no kinship with the concepts that make known the perfection of the mystery of Christ, that is, the divine mystery itself of the Word's becoming man. It was not far off, or rather some were already muttering under their breath, that even the holy council at Chalcedon should be set aside, as being bound up with that council according to the

…as in truth, he pressed us to send letters to your brotherly blessedness in keeping with the aim of his drunken madness. In response to this, how we used the language of accommodation, so as to fend off the tyrannical and unyielding pressure and to reduce the absurdity to something more moderate—knowing that choosing between evils is not wholly to be rejected when it is not possible to hold fast purely to the good itself in the first place—this will be attested for us by the Power that watches over the counsels of the heart; and among men, by the God-beloved apocrisiarius of your most holy see who resides here, whom, at the very height of the crisis, we informed truthfully and on oath, making plain to him our sincere disposition toward orthodoxy. For you too know, most holy ones, having learned it clearly by experience, how [?] very resistant and

…always healing what is weak and filling up what is lacking, transfers Germanus, the most holy [?] bishop of the metropolis of Cyzicus, to be archbishop of this God-guarded and imperial city. Under the emperor Artemius [?]
…until the 4th year of Philippicus, a mad synod took place against the holy sixth ecumenical council; and Cyrus having been expelled in the 6th year of his patriarchate…

…to be harsh toward the compulsion of power in such matters is easy, requiring no skill or ingenuity. After all, even Nathan the prophet did not bring his rebuke about the adultery and the murder to David undisguised, although David himself had been honored with the prophetic gift. In the same way we too, as the great Basil says, consented to yield a little to the man's temper, so that the confession of the faith on its critical points might be kept inviolate, if not in its words, at least in its meaning. "For truth for us lies not in words but in realities," as the divine Gregory cries out. And again, he declares, "It is quite absurd and very shameful to quibble over sounds." And the apostolic Dionysius the Areopagite pronounces it "irrational and foolish to pay attention not to the force of the intention but to the words; and this," he says, "is not characteristic of those who wish to understand divine things, but of those who accept bare sounds and keep them outside, letting them go no further than the ears, and who do not wish to know what a given word signifies, or how it ought to be explained through other words of equal force and greater clarity." We say this not as wishing to overturn the expressions already defined synodically and confessed by the whole Church of God for so long a time—that is, to speak, concerning the mystery of Christ's incarnation, of two natural wills and two natural operations, in the pious sense familiar to the holy Fathers—but looking only to the tyrant's "persuasion," as the Apostle calls it, and to its being by a stratagem

[?] …John became patriarch of Constantinople, and Andrew metropolitan of Crete, and Germanus metropolitan of Cyzicus (who evidently signed, along with others in those same times, and anathematized the aforementioned holy ecumenical council held against the Monothelites). After three years, when John died, Germanus was transferred from Cyzicus and was patriarch of Constantinople for 15 years. [?]

turned to the opposite, so that alien doctrines might not be openly introduced into the Church, and the decrees of true religion on the matter at hand, which had been well established and had remained unshaken, might not be utterly overthrown; and at the same time counting it a great thing that the teaching of the said holy council should be confessed in its meaning even by the council's enemies. Hence the very things the tyrant contrived against the council clearly show not its overthrow but rather its confirmation, at least to those who know how to examine such matters with a sound and impartial eye of understanding. For to say that Christ wills and acts according to each nature is nothing other than to understand two natural wills and two natural operations. For the holy council assembled in your great city of Rome under Martin of venerable memory, who presided over your Church, expressly laid down in the definition it pronounced that such expressions are to be understood in this sense. So the wisdom of God, who catches the wise in their own craftiness, clearly arranged things in our case too, sinful and least as we are, just as Gregory the Theologian relates in his funeral oration on the great Basil, where he presents him as taking the divine David for his counselor and ordering his words with discretion: he kept silent about the proper term concerning the Holy Spirit, but strengthened the pious preaching of the faith with other terms that could mean the same thing. And yet no one, I think, is unaware how great the difference is between the two subjects—I mean faith and confession concerning the Godhead itself, and the concerns about the divine incarnation, as the same Gregory the Theologian among the saints puts it, all that the detailed inquiry necessarily requires to demonstrate the perfection according to each nature—[?] since the words and doctrines concerning the divine nature, that is, the life-giving Trinity, rather hold precedence, as being more exalted and more to be honored. For this is how we have understood what the same wise Theologian said against the Eunomians in his discourse on theology, where he says: "Philosophize for me about the world, about matter, about the soul, about rational natures both better and worse, about the resurrection,

“For in these matters it is not useless to hit the mark, and it is not dangerous to miss it.” The teacher did not say this simply and without qualification. He said it by way of contrast with what is said and taught as doctrine about the divine Trinity. We are convinced, most holy ones, that the rest of what happened also came about through this kind of accommodation, made by economy and because of circumstances. So do not agree to bring an unpardonable charge against us for these things. Even if we are suspected of having fallen short of strict correctness, let that be set beside what our holy Fathers did by economy, and so be acquitted, not liable to account and free of all condemnation. Even the most wise Cyril advised, for the sake of economy, that Theodore of Mopsuestia should not be expressly condemned, as a concession to those who were still weaker on this point, although he knew Theodore to be the originator and father of Nestorius's false teaching. What he wrote about this to Proclus, now among the saints, who presided over our most holy Church, shows this. The tyrant of the faith mentioned above, whose own conscience was seared, as the most holy Paul says, dared to burn the volumes of the acts of the celebrated holy sixth synod that were kept in the palace. He thought, in his own opinion, that he would wipe out the word of truth along with them. We left him to be deceived by his own conceit and to boast of his own shame as though it were some great achievement. Meanwhile we carefully kept safe the volumes of the acts of the celebrated holy sixth synod held by us. In these, the signatures of all the bishops who met at that holy synod, together with the emperor's subscription, are contained in the definition it issued. In our time the acts of the same holy synod have also been kept free of corruption in another way, through still more careful effort. By the grace of God we hold the autograph book of Paul of holy memory, who became president of our most holy Church and who served at that synod as an asecretis. So the Church of God will be secure in time to come as well. No one at all, out of malice, will dare to falsify the acts of the holy sixth synod, carried out continuously as stated before, or be able wickedly to attribute such things to others, for time tends to bring many innovations among people. The unaltered and genuine character of the truth will be shown to everyone still more clearly from this book. Our true Master and Saviour, the Lord Jesus Christ, did not put up with sleeping for long in patience over these things. He arose, by his own goodness and power, and now too re-

buked the surge, not of water this time, but of a lawless undertaking. He stilled the storm and turmoil of the Churches and gave us a great calm in our affairs: a pious emperor, virtuous in every way, equal to and worthy of the height of empire, who has zeal for orthodoxy and good order in his ways of life, and who, true to his name, has raised up again for us the peace and concord of the Church. We trust in the One who gave him to us that, as his name foretells, he is also the beginning of a raising up of the affairs of the state. You, then, O sacred head, through the most discerning power of the Spirit within you, stretch out to us the hand of a kindly appeal [?] by the gentle touch of letters in reply, according to the custom of the Church, that is, by sending synodical letters in return. Apply the medicine of love and be eager to heal what pains us and throbs within us. For there is no relief for the soul, nor will sleep come to the eyes, nor rest to the temples, nor slumber to our eyelids, until we see the universal Church of God once again preserving the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace. You are disciples and successors of the one who heard from the Lord: “Simon, Simon, look, Satan has demanded to sift you like wheat. But I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail. And you, when you have turned back, strengthen your brothers.” So, God-honoured ones, you are obliged on the one hand to apply diligently the strengthening that leads to correction, and on the other to grant all the more readily the favour of a sympathetic mind. The Lord urged the chief of the apostles himself, from his own experience, to understand the weakness of the flesh. He was not to cut off from restoration through correction to their former steadfastness those who had suffered a slip and a fall under pressure from outside, just as he himself had suffered at the time of the saving Passion. And do not let your sacred memory forget this. Some of those who deposed the impious Eutyches under Flavian of holy memory later, at the synod held in Ephesus under Dioscorus, declared the justly condemned man innocent and laid a most unjust condemnation on the most blessed Flavian. Yet at the holy synod of Chalcedon, drawing up a sound confession was enough for them to remove the charge completely, and they did not need much labour or many words for it. For brotherly affection knows not to put off for long its gentleness and kindness toward one's neighbour. These things, to those gathered at Chalcedon itself, [? variant readings: … “to be deprived”]

Fathers, the most holy Leo laid down. He was the most brilliant lamp of your apostolic see, or rather of the whole world, and he wrote as follows: “But since many things often happen that can produce repentance, and the mercy of God overcomes the offences of sinners, punishment is held in suspense, so that there may be room for correction.” Again, writing to Pulcheria of pious memory in a letter that begins, “The God-loving care of your clemency, which you unceasingly devote to the catholic faith,” Leo's most princely mind says this: “As I have written very often from the beginning of this affair, I want this clemency to be preserved amid both divided minds and carnal jealousies. Nothing may be added to the perfection of the faith, nor anything taken away from it, but the remedy of pardon should be given to those who return to unity and peace. For the works of the devil are destroyed most powerfully when human hearts are called back to the love of God and of neighbour.” Long before this, Cyril, who was exact in divine matters, is found to have done this very thing when the Eastern bishops quarrelled with him and opposed him. Wanting to release Nestorius from his condemnation and hurrying to cancel the verdict against him, they dared intolerable things and committed a very grave offence, for they anathematized the blessed Cyril himself and his synod. Yet he brought them back quickly and without difficulty, simply by their agreeing to what had been decreed in synod and piously defined and confirming the condemnation of the impious man. At this the same God-bearing Father cried out those words full of every joy, which one might suppose were spoken as though he himself had been pardoned a fault, rather than having pardoned those who had erred: “Let the heavens rejoice and the earth be glad, for the dividing wall of the barrier has been broken down and every form of discord has been removed, since Christ, the Saviour of us all, has granted peace to his Churches.” You too, then, O God-inspired ones, have a defence that cancels the error committed under compulsion. It is strong and lawful and can in no way be overturned: the pure and openly spoken confession of orthodoxy. So, blessed ones, do not be slow and hesitant to be joined with us, inseparable in spiritual harmony and concord. Do not dwell on what was done under force and thrust away from your love us who were forced. Do not regard us as enemies, as the divine Apostle says, but admonish us as brothers, and so show an imitation of God. Surely, most holy ones, you will conclude from the scriptural account of Aaron, the holy one of the Lord,

as the divine Spirit proclaimed him, that a just pardon follows for things done under compulsion and not out of deliberate wickedness of mind. This holds unless it is a case of total denial and of being led into complete godlessness. That Aaron gave way to the impulse of the people of old and helped them carry out the making of the idol, and his brother reproached him for it. But he pleaded compulsion and force in his defence, and he received not a single rebuke from God, nor was he stripped of the dignity of the high priesthood. For the One who fashioned our hearts one by one, as the great David says, looked wholly to what was genuine in his inner disposition toward divine worship, and not to his outward misfortune. Our mind's soundness and natural agreement with right doctrine has now been shown, together with our readiness, without delay, to condemn what was wrongly done and to establish the doctrines of true religion by confirming the said holy sixth synod. So embrace us, most honoured brothers. For the divine Apostle cries out to us at the top of his voice, “Bear one another's burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ,” so that with one accord, in one spirit, we may glorify the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ.
